In 9D, LYE is described as [an *aid* in making soap]. Now, my understanding is that soap, at its core, is a salt between a fatty acid, such as stearic, and an alkali ion, such as sodium or potassium. The sodium comes from lye [NaOH]. So in that sense, lye is an ingredient--a reagent--not an aid, which participates but doesn't join in--a solvent or catalyst.

Of course, you could substitute the lye with something else, like potassium hydroxide, but that would be making pie crust with lard instead of butter.

Old backpacker's tip: wanna clean out that dirty cook pot? Throw a little ash from the campfire in--the potash from the ash will cause saponification (How I love that word--Robyn, I miss you*!) with the fats in the pan, and grit from the ash will provide abrasive. In fact "pot ash"-->"potassium," which is why we call it that in English, unlike the "Kalium" of other, benighted, languages.

*a dearly-missed friend, who was a high school science teacher, not Robyn Weintraub. But, Ms. Wientraub, if you're reading, please include SAPONIFICATION into a late-week grid!

Despite being an (aging) gym-bunny, I had difficulty making the leap between [Swoleness] to BULK--the difference between abstract vs. concrete--"bulkiness" vs. "bulk." But I wish the haters would stop dissing "swole"--what a wonderful word, one which displays the true vitality of the English language! Among the various dictionaries I regularly consult, the OED only lists "swole" as an archaic variant past form of "to swell.' Same with the University of Michigan's Middle English Compendium (because everyone in A2 speaks like Chaucer--trust me, I've been there.) "Swole" had made it into M-W online, with a few citations, as well as Green's Dictionary of Slang. But no "swoleness" in either. No, for "swoleness," one must turn to the Urban Dictionary: "the state of being swole, ripped buff." The Urban dictionary includes other derivations, including "swolefest," "swolesesh," and even "Swoleversary": "The annual recurrence of a date marking when you decided to stop being a little b and started hitting the gym and changed your life in a positive manner. And got swole as f.: 'Dave: Yo Steve! Looking pretty swole bro!' 'Steve: Thanks bro, yesterday was my Swoleversary! I can't believe I've been lifting for 3 years already!' Curiously, even the Urban Dictionary misses "swolfie": taking a picture of one's self at the gym, while totally pumped, to then share on social media. (Been there, done that.) https://www.urbandictionary.com/define.php?term=swoleness

@Megan This. Literally the meaning of the word is "hook" in French - I'm surprised that anyone who knows the word "crochet" enough to include it in a crossword puzzle would make that mistake.

@Megan You are 100% correct, but... The clue says "Needle-working," not "needle" itself. Apparently, even though CROCHET uses a hook and not a needle, it can fall under the category of "needlework," according to some authorities: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needlework https://www.indooroutdoors.co.uk/blogs/news/different-types-of-needlework-sewing-crochet-and-knitting (Note the wiggle words "hooked needle.") Even Britannica agrees: https://kids.britannica.com/students/article/needlework/276047 Much like hot dogs, which are called dogs, but no actual dogs are harmed in their creation. The only quibble I see is that there shouldn't be a hyphen there; it makes it look more like it involves an actual needle.

@Steve L

Needlework and needle-work are different-- to me, the second implies working with literal needles. So I'm with the people saying it's a bad clue, especially for a Monday.

@Isabeau it feels almost intentional - it would have been easy enough to use the phrase "fiber art" and avoid the complaints altogether. Calling it needlecraft doesn't make it easier or harder; it just annoys the crocheters. And if the constructor (or the editors, for that matter) consulted even a single crocheter, they would know that this was going to annoy the crocheters.

@Isabeau

As I said in my comment, the hyphen is the only quibble here.  In reality, "needle-work" with the hyphen isn't really a thing; Google it, and every hit comes back "needlework."  Google "needle-working," and you either get "needlework" or "needle working."  The hyphen just doesn't belong there.  

Without any dictionary definitions, the slightly off-kilter "needle-working" can mean whatever you think it means.  Certainly crocheters can be upset; there's actually a term of art for this:  TCS (Too Close Syndrome).  It refers to when someone is so involved in a certain field that they can't step back and see what the general public can:  that crocheting is considered needlework by the average Joe (or perhaps Jane), and the hyphen doesn't really change things.

The only other quibble is that on a Monday, the clues should probably be much more straightforward.

One other thing:  You object that "needle-work" should refer to actual needles.  Do you disagree with the several sources that the crocheting implement is a "hooked needle"?

@Isabeau

OK, fair enough, but if several sources call it a "hooked needle," that means that it's sometimes called that, doesn't it, and as a result, it's fine for the clue?

(This is where it's no longer an opinion, because I'm thinking like a crossword editor and not a crocheter.  Do you see my point?)

(Note that I said that I agreed with Megan's original statement.)

I understand that as a crocheter, you "feel" that the clue is wrong, but there's evidence that it still works.

@Isabeau

OK, so then would you agree that despite your assessment above, that if several sources in the field allow it, the clue is valid?

(At this point, it stops becoming an opinion.  It's clear that this is how crossword clues are derived, and this one, though a bit tricky for a Monday, falls within the limits of the "rules" of cluing.)

@Bill

Excellent question!  

My view is that "aid" is not really a chemical term--what you're getting at with "participates in but does not join in" would be a catalyst.  

Catalysts are unaffected by the overall reaction, although they do play a part in making a reaction go faster at a given temperature.  Enzymes are a particular class of catalysts that are made of protein.  Almost every chemical reaction in a living system is modulated by an enzyme, and they can make a reaction happen millions of times faster than without the catalyst.  A single enzyme molecule can produce millions of reaction products per second, like a super-fast machine splitting out product.

In theory the entirety of the mass of catalyst added to a reaction can be isolated after the reaction, completely unchanged.  

In this case, I'd say that the lye, a strong base like NaOH or KOH (sodium or potassium hydroxides) reacts with an organic carboxylic acid, like oleic or stearic acids, neutralizing the acid *and* the base, resulting in an kind of salt with a Na+ or K+ ion, and an anion (negatively charged ion) that keeps everything electrically neutral.  (It also works with calcium hydroxide and the other alkaline earth metals.)

Aren't you glad you asked?  You guys should really appreciate the character limit when eliciting a post from a former professor who can't say anything in less than a thousand characters.

@Leon

In some situations, an estimate is actually the quoted price for a job.  The only way the price would change is if the customer requests something different, mid-job.

In some situations, an estimate may change when something hidden is discovered, and the original job cannot be completed safely without the additional work.  Like replacing a deck and discovering that the wood it is attached to is rotting, and needs to be replaced.  (Ask me how I know.)

A guesstimate is just a round figure offered by someone who hasn't thoroughly inspected the site or when there are variables that are unknown.  Like when you want to get new windows, but all you know is you have 15 of them to replace, and they're average-sized.  Or how much it would cost a landscaper to design your entire unplanted yard before you pick out the plantings.

Hope that helps!
